sections.title: Contributions and acknowledgements

summary.text: Acknowledges the experts, advisors, reviewers, and production team who contributed to the guide under the WHO Health Workforce Department, and credits financial support from the Government of Japan and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID).

sections.extract: Under the direction of the World Health Organization (WHO) Health Workforce Department, this Implementation Guide has been developed as an accompanying document to the National Health Workforce Accounts Handbook, to support the implementation of the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030. WHO is grateful to the following experts and advisors who provided guidance and technical input: Mathieu

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces the policy mandate for National Health Workforce Accounts (WHA69.19, WHA70.6, and the UN High-Level Commission on Health Employment and Economic Growth) and explains how the NHWA health labour market framework, 10-module Handbook, and online platform support countries in integrating multisectoral HRH data.

sections.extract: Introduction With the objective to accelerate progress towards universal health coverage, and to facilitate adoption of the Global strategy on human resources for health: Workforce 2030 (1), the Sixty- ninth World Health Assembly resolution WHA69.19 (2) in 2016 urged all Member States to consolidate “a core set of human resources for health data […] as well as progressive imple- mentation of national health

sections.title: Purpose of this Guide

summary.text: States the purpose of the Implementation Guide: providing recommendations to help Member States systematically gather and use standardized, sustainable human resources for health (HRH) information to understand health workforce dynamics.

sections.extract: Member States need a comprehensive overview of the dynamics of their health workforce. The Guide proposes recommendations that enable countries to develop or improve systematic gath- ering and use of relevant HRH information in a sustainable and standardized manner to achieve this goal.

sections.title: Target audience

summary.text: Identifies the primary target audiences for the guide, including Ministry of Health HRH policy-makers and programme managers, officials across education, labour, finance, civil service, and national statistical bodies, professional councils, international advisors, and HRH researchers.

sections.extract: The document is primarily addressed to: • Policy-makers and programme managers involved in HRH policy and strategy in the Ministry of Health, or bodies delegated to undertake this function. • Policy-makers, officials and programme managers in relevant areas such as education, employment and labour, social affairs and economy and finance; civil service commissions, statistical organizations and institutes for health

sections.title: Guiding principles

summary.text: Outlines four guiding principles for NHWA implementation: retaining existing national HRH terminology where appropriate, fostering collaborative multisectoral stakeholder responsibility, following a systematic "do-no-harm" approach harmonized with existing health information systems, and complementing rather than replacing existing structures.

sections.extract: The following key guiding principles should be borne in mind when reading this document. • NHWA terminology is proposed throughout this document, but need not replace existing terminology that describes the HRH information system, such as HRH registries, health workforce observatories or other equivalent systems. • To be effective, activities to strengthen HRH data within the NHWA framework should be collaborative,

sections.title: How to use this Guide

summary.text: Explains how Member States can flexibly apply and order the guide's proposed steps according to the maturity of their existing national HRH information frameworks and coordination needs.

sections.extract: How to use this Guide • The Guide can be used to check whether health workforce data, reporting objectives and tasks can be achieved within the existing national framework, and whether the latter requires adaptations to align with the NHWA principles and framework. • In Member States where all or many elements of the NHWA Guide already exist, there may only be a need for coordination, networking and a communication

sections.title: NHWA implementation structure overview

summary.text: Presents the three-phase, eight-step NHWA implementation structure (Figure 1): Phase I (Conceptualization) to define governance and partners, Phase II (Operationalization) to elaborate workflows, legal clearances, and data aggregation, and Phase III (Process revision and sustainability) to mainstream and update the system.

sections.extract: Eight steps are proposed over three phases to strengthen HRH data monitoring and to report on HRH at national and international level, such as to WHO (Figure 1). The conceptualization phase defines the NHWA framework and governance, and identifies key partners who will constitute a working group to monitor, analyse and report health workforce statistics. sections.title: Summary of steps

summary.text: Summarizes the eight implementation steps across the three phases (Figure 2): Steps 1–3 for conceptualization (governmental buy-in, governance, scoping and planning), Steps 4–7 for routine operationalization (legal framework, data compilation and analysis, validation, dissemination), and Step 8 for periodic process revision.

sections.title: Schedule for implementing and reporting on NHWA

summary.text: Notes that national NHWA implementation planning should align with the reporting periodicity specified in the NHWA Handbook, where most indicators are monitored annually and others every three years.

sections.extract: Member States will need to plan for implementation of the NHWA. In particular, in cases where the process requires changes, the planning should consider the timing of reporting as described in the NHWA Handbook for each indicator. Most indicators require annual moni- toring, while others may be reported every three years.

sections.title: Bodies and roles

summary.text: Describes the five key organizational bodies and roles involved in national NHWA implementation—the Ministry of Health focal point, multistakeholder coordination working group, secretariat, technical working group, and communications team—and notes how participants may hold overlapping roles.

sections.extract: While this Guide provides an indicative list of entities that may be involved in implementing the NHWA, it should be adapted to suit Member States’ particular circumstances and struc- tures. • Ministry of Health focal point: a person or body in charge of HRH within a Member State’s government. sections.title: Overview of NHWA implementation

summary.text: Provides a consolidated reference summary of the objectives, tasks and activities, and main outputs for each of the eight NHWA implementation steps across conceptualization, operationalization, and process revision.

sections.extract: Step 1: Governmental “buy-in” Objectives • Obtain political commitment to strengthen HRH data • Ensure adoption of the NHWA framework by the Ministry of Health • Fulfil initial steps to coordinate intersectoral health workforce agenda Tasks and activities • A health workforce representative within the Ministry of Health is identified to become the NHWA focal point • All available support resources are grouped

sections.title: Step 1. Governmental “buy-in”

summary.text: Details Step 1 (Governmental "buy-in") in Phase I, describing how the Ministry of Health appoints an empowered NHWA focal point, assesses existing HRH systems, engages intersectoral ministries and WHO offices, and secures ministerial adoption of a long-term implementation plan.

sections.extract: To move towards the delivery of NHWA, it is essential that Member States show significant political commitment and strong national leadership. This commitment will normally come from the Ministry of Health, who will develop a plan to strengthen HRH data using the NHWA frame- work. The creation and adoption of any plan to strengthen HRH data capture will normally be led by an appointed focal point within the Ministry

sections.title: Step 2. Governance

summary.text: Details Step 2 (Governance) in Phase I, covering stakeholder mapping, establishing a multisectoral coordination working group with written terms of reference and accountability lines, nominating the secretariat and technical working group, and agreeing on key HRH policy questions.

sections.extract: Governance The purpose of the multistakeholder, multisectoral working group is to coordinate NHWA implementation and strengthen HRH data. This working group will build as much as possible on existing structures and mechanisms such as HRH units, observatories and committees, as well as any other committee involved in collecting and reporting of HRH or related data. sections.title: Step 3. Scoping and planning

summary.text: Details Step 3 (Scoping and planning) in Phase I, guiding the technical and multistakeholder working groups in mapping HRH data sources and gaps, assessing IT interoperability and platform maturity, prioritizing indicator sources, preparing analysis and dissemination plans, and costing a business plan with catalytic and rolling budgets.

sections.extract: During the scoping and planning step, the technical working group will map available data and data systems in the country and will elaborate a plan for any additional HRH data gath- ering. From the key policy questions defined in step 2, core indicators should be defined before collecting data. sections.title: Step 4. Legal framework

summary.text: Details Step 4 (Legal framework) in Phase II, explaining how the secretariat and stakeholders assess national data protection and ethics regulations, obtain formal authorizations for data extraction and anonymization, and adopt standard operating procedures (SOPs) including a data breach mitigation plan.

sections.extract: Legal framework Understanding the legal framework or environment that exists in the country, and how it impacts on HRH data collection, analysis and use, is essential. Failure to do so at an early stage can lead to wasted time and resources. This step is required to ensure that the NHWA activity led by the multistakeholder working group can operate legally. sections.title: Step 5. Data compilation and analysis

summary.text: Details Step 5 (Data compilation and analysis) in Phase II, describing how the technical working group and secretariat assess source quality, harmonize indicator definitions and metadata, centralize aggregated data from focal points via national or WHO NHWA platforms, and plan strategies to address data gaps.

sections.extract: This step considers data collection and managing data from multiple sources. Data are analysed according to the plan defined in step 3 in order to answer key policy questions and to identify potential data gaps. sections.title: Step 6. Validation

summary.text: Details Step 6 (Validation) in Phase II, outlining how the technical working group and secretariat synthesize indicator findings for workshops and executive review so the multistakeholder working group can formally validate the NHWA analysis, adopt a national HRH report, and tailor key messages for decision-makers.

sections.extract: Validation Validation of the data and information produced is essential. At this step, the technical working group will translate the data to help the multistakeholder working group interpret and under- stand the implication of the findings and develop recommendations based on the analyses. The multistakeholder working group will define which key messages should be disseminated to decision-makers in various sectors

sections.title: Step 7. Dissemination

summary.text: Details Step 7 (Dissemination) in Phase II, covering how the multistakeholder working group, secretariat, and communications team distribute national HRH reports, policy briefs, scientific publications, and authorized public data while tracking message uptake across target audiences.

sections.extract: Dissemination The use of HRH information collected with the NHWA will lead to a series of findings, with impli- cations for stakeholders and the general public. A cogent and realistic communication plan is essential to guide the dissemination of findings to target groups and relevant bodies, including academia, nationally and internationally. sections.title: Step 8. Process revision

summary.text: Details Step 8 (Process revision) in Phase III, describing periodic strategic reviews of Steps 1–7 by the multistakeholder working group to evaluate lessons learned, update governance and indicator sets, onboard new stakeholders, and secure sustainable regular funding.

sections.extract: Process revision This step reviews the work conducted to gather, interpret and disseminate HRH information as part of the NHWA. The purpose is to understand the strengths and weaknesses of the processes used and identify improvements to help the progressive and sustainable implementation of HRH data monitoring using the NHWA framework.
